posts.text: Why you should learn the full robotics software stack, not just one tool Are you an entry-level Robotics Software Engineer, or a student who has built a few robot projects? Here is a hard truth. Most robots that work in a demo fail in the real world. The reason is rarely the hardware. It is the software around it. Recruiters hiring for robotics roles in 2026 look for people who understand how the pieces connect. Here is what that stack looks like, and why each layer matters: 🔹 ROS 2: The backbone of modern robots. Nodes, topics, services and launch files are how real robot systems talk to each other. If you know ROS 2 well, you can join almost any robotics team. 🔹 Simulation (Gazebo, Isaac Sim): Test before you break hardware. A digital twin lets you stream LiDAR, cameras and IMU data and try out ideas safely. It is also where most industry testing happens now. 🔹 State estimation and perception: Sensors are noisy. Fusing them into one reliable pose, and turning a camera feed into a target, is what separates a toy from a robot you can trust. 🔹 SLAM and Navigation (Nav2): Mapping a space, planning a route and avoiding people and obstacles. This is core to warehouse, logistics and service robotics. 🔹 Manipulation (MoveIt 2): Motion planning for robot arms. Locate, pick, deliver. This is where many Physical AI jobs are heading. 🔹 Testing and failure analysis: The skill nobody teaches. Real engineers inject faults on purpose (sensor dropout, blocked paths, slipped grasps), measure what breaks, and fix it with evidence. Tracking error, latency, localisation drift, mission success rate. Numbers, not opinions. 💡 The takeaway: Do not learn these as separate tutorials. Build one robot and keep adding to it, layer by layer, until it runs a full autonomous mission. That is the project that gets you hired. 🎓 This is how we built the Quanskill Robotics Systems Level 2 course. It is 12 weeks online, one robot with a new skill every week, and strong graduates move on to a 3-month internship with QuanRobotics. The first batch starts in November, and each batch has only 10 seats. posts.text: 1969. Houston, United States. A team of scientists and engineers is preparing a mission that will take human beings to the Moon. Among them is a remarkable woman: Margaret Hamilton, Director of the Software Engineering Division for the Apollo programme. At the time, software engineering is still an emerging discipline. Yet Hamilton understands something fundamental: The success of a complex project does not depend on one individual, but on the ability to bring different areas of expertise together. She champions rigour, anticipates potential failures and insists on preparing for the unexpected. During the Apollo 11 mission, computer overload alarms threaten the lunar landing. But the software has been designed to prioritise critical tasks, allowing the crew to continue their mission. This achievement is no stroke of luck. It is the result of collective effort, clear vision and trust in the expertise of others. Her story offers a powerful management lesson: You can lead a complex project without being the person who knows every technical detail. Even today, some managers believe they must be the most competent person on their team. What a mistake! Hiring someone more talented than you is not a threat. Listening to your colleagues is not a sign of weakness. Surrounding yourself with strong personalities does not diminish your authority. Acknowledging your limitations does not undermine your leadership. A mediocre manager wants to be the smartest person in the room. A great manager wants to bring the smartest minds around the table. Shine on ✨

Recently, I had the opportunity to attend Walmart’s flagship tech conference, 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲, and listen to inspiring speakers discuss AI adoption, its impact, future possibilities, and the risks that come with its rapid growth. One thought stayed with me. As organisations race to adopt AI, improve productivity, and build leaner teams, are we overlooking the future of fresh talent? AI can now write code, generate tests, and speed up development. Experienced engineers are increasingly focusing on architecture, reviewing AI-generated code, and making complex technical decisions. A few facts worth reflecting on: • Stanford research: Employment among software developers aged 22–25 declined nearly 20% from its late-2022 peak through 2025, according to research on early-career employment and AI exposure. • Gartner (2026): Its survey found that some organisations have stopped hiring for certain entry-level roles because of AI automation. • Industry shift: As AI takes on more routine coding and testing, the expectations from engineers are changing towards broader ownership, system design, and technical judgement. These trends raise an important question. If fresh graduates get fewer opportunities to learn by doing, where will tomorrow’s experienced engineers come from? Engineering judgement, architecture, and problem-solving don’t develop overnight. They come from hands-on experience, learning from mistakes, and mentorship. The answer isn’t to slow down AI adoption. It’s to rethink how we develop talent alongside it — helping fresh graduates learn to build with AI, not simply expecting AI to replace the learning process. posts.text: What if you could test a development policy on 600 people before rolling it out to millions? Click any person to follow their story. 5⃣ Compare scenarios See who benefits, who stays vulnerable, and why. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 Averages hide people. A program can raise average income and still leave the most vulnerable behind. A digital twin shows these trade-offs before resources are committed — not after. He is a business developer who combines product strategy, software development and partnership building. Turning a complex policy idea into a tool anyone can explore in minutes takes rare talent. 💡 Looking for someone who turns ideas into products? Visit Alexander Odere's profile and connect. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗘𝗴𝘆𝗽𝘁 + 𝗞𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗮 Having worked with low-income households at Nasser Social Bank in Aswan, and now pursuing a PhD in Development Policy at KDI School in Korea, I see real value in tools that connect evidence from the ground with Korea's strength in evidence-based policy — adaptable to any region in the world. posts.text: Software agencies died in 2026. That’s what the internet keeps telling us. So I went through the arguments. Take 1: No. AI hasn’t killed agencies. It changed what developers do. Take 2: No. AI lets people solve problems faster without paying developers, designers and agencies a fortune. Take 3: Yes. Why hire five people when one person with AI can do the work? Take 4: Hell no. A ChatGPT employee says AI is trying to take over the world, so we’re all doomed anyway. Funny. But the job market tells a less funny story. The numbers: US software developer job postings fell 73% from their February 2022 peak to February 2025, according to Indeed data cited by Investopedia. They’ve rebounded since but are still below pre-pandemic levels. The World Economic Forum projects 92 million jobs displaced globally by 2030 and 170 million created. That covers the whole economy, not just AI. Juniors have it worst. AI handles more coding tasks, but companies still need experienced engineers to make architectural decisions, review code and solve hard problems. Entry-level roles are under pressure while senior demand shows signs of recovery. AI doesn’t need to replace every developer to disrupt the industry. It only needs to let a company do the same work with fewer people. A project that needed six people might now need three who use AI well. A client who used to hire an agency might build an MVP with one AI-savvy founder. A small agency that competed on cheap development might have nothing left to compete on. Jobs rarely disappear with an announcement. Companies just stop hiring for them. So are software agencies finished? No. But agencies that sell code as their main value have a serious problem. The ones that last will understand the client’s business problem, build reliable systems, own the outcome and use AI to deliver more with less. The others may not notice until the pipeline dries up. How much of today’s work will still need a human tomorrow? For agencies, we’re already finding out. I have a strong case study but have got no more energy to write, good night!

posts.text: JetBrains open-sourced a 12B coding model yesterday that fixes 47% of real GitHub issues with only 2.5B parameters active per token. It's like hiring a junior who reads the repo, runs the tests, and checks their own diff before handing it back — instead of paying a frontier model for every line. Mellum2.1 (Apache 2.0, 131k context) got there through RL, not scale: post-training ran millions of sandboxed runs across thousands of real environments. JetBrains' own numbers: 47.0% SWE-bench Verified, 28.0% SWE-bench Pro. For comparison, Microsoft's MAI Code 1.1 scores 72.6% in the cloud and 70.8% on-device — the frontier still leads by ~26 points. But Mellum2.1 was the fastest in its test group under load, serving almost 2x the tokens/sec of Qwen3.5-9B on one H200, and it runs entirely on your own hardware. Best for: self-hosted sub-agents and high-volume repo work where code can't leave your machines. Not for: the hardest multi-file refactors. posts.headline: Co-Founder & CRO Prismus | Turning technical signals into commercial opportunities
posts.text: My clients and I have more in common than I initially thought. Many are scientists, engineers or founders. They build and sell complex hardware or software into lab settings. And while our products are very different, we are all trying to figure out the same things. Is there a real need? Am I talking to the right person? Do they have budget? Is now a good time? Basically, the good old BANT framework: Budget, Authority, Need, Timing. What’s different is where we look for answers. For our clients, that often means digging into scientific papers, grants, conference presentations, technical hiring or company announcements. Trying to understand what people are actually working on in their labs. And whether their technology could be relevant. For me, the signals are a bit different. But I’m asking pretty much the same questions. And yes, I use Prismus.ai myself to find and qualify opportunities. Eating our own dog food. 😄 Finding prospects is one thing. Figuring out who to approach, why and when is the tricky part. What signals tell you that a prospect is worth reaching out to?
